prompt.context: A Contact Lens Manufacturer seeks to quadruple its profits in 2 years and has engaged our firm for advice.
prompt.question: The client wants to quadruple its profits within 2 years. How will you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What are the different kinds of contact lenses?
clarifying_info.a: Contact lenses can be categorized by style (Traditional vs. Cosmetic) and by duration of use (Disposable vs. Regular).

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of contact lenses?
clarifying_info.a: Disposable lenses: consumers pay $400 per year. Regular lenses: consumers pay $100 per year.
There are 2 major competitors: Novartis and Bausch & Lomb. They are big players with a wide array of products.
Not much differentiation; products are very similar.

clarifying_info.q: How do customers decide what brand to use?
clarifying_info.a: New adopters: the optometrist typically influences the brand decision; the customer plays a minimal role. Existing users: they tend to keep using the same brand and rarely switch.

clarifying_info.q: How do customers purchase contact lenses?
clarifying_info.a: New adopters go to a retail store, get an eye exam, and the doctor or optometrist recommends a lens. Existing users place refill orders from retail stores or online.
Western Europe and Japan are large markets outside the US, but competitors are deeply entrenched there and the client has little presence. Other markets are still small. Detailed data is limited.

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's current margins relative to industry?
clarifying_info.a: Margins are more or less in line with the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Is there opportunity in the Regular lens market?
clarifying_info.a: The Regular contact lens market is saturated.

clarifying_info.q: Is there opportunity in the Cosmetic lens market?
clarifying_info.a: The Cosmetic market is not estimated to grow much.

clarifying_info.q: Why are sales lower in the South region of the US?
clarifying_info.a: The client's presence in Southern United States is smaller.

exhibits.title: Contact Lens Manufacturer Income Statement
exhibits.shows: Income statement for the contact lens manufacturer showing revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, SG&A, D&A, operating income, non-operating items, and net income (all in millions of USD)

exhibits.title: Revenue by Region
exhibits.shows: Chart or table displaying the client's revenue broken down by US geographic region
exhibits.data: Exact figures visible in image; South region sales appear notably lower than other regions

exhibits.title: Revenue by Product Mix
exhibits.shows: Chart or table displaying the client's revenue broken down by product category (Traditional vs. Cosmetic and/or Disposable vs. Regular)
exhibits.data: Exact figures visible in image; product mix is predominantly Disposable and Traditional

exhibits.title: Total Contact Lens Users by Demographic
exhibits.shows: Chart showing total contact lens users (new adopters plus existing users) by demographic segment (e.g., age, gender, geography)
exhibits.data: Exact figures visible in image; represents total users, not new adopters alone

exhibits.title: New Adopters by Demographic — Age/Gender
exhibits.shows: Chart showing new contact lens adopters segmented by age and/or gender

exhibits.title: New Adopters by Demographic — Geography/Growth
exhibits.shows: Chart showing new contact lens adopters segmented by US geography and growth rate

exhibits.title: New Adopters — Additional Demographic Breakdown
exhibits.shows: Chart providing further demographic breakdown of new adopters

exhibits.title: New Adopters — Store/Location Characteristics
exhibits.shows: Chart or data relating to where new adopters purchase lenses or characteristics of relevant retail locations

framework: Client's current revenue model and financial baseline — understand current profits and what quadrupling implies in revenue terms
Competitor analysis — who are the major players, how differentiated are products, what market positions do they hold
Market analysis — total market size, growth trends, segmentation by product type (Traditional/Cosmetic, Disposable/Regular)
Geography — regional breakdown of current sales and where growth opportunities exist
Customer demographics — who buys contact lenses and which segments are growing fastest
Purchase criteria and purchase process — how customers choose brands and what influences the buying decision
Top-line growth levers — given cost reduction alone cannot quadruple profits in 2 years, focus on revenue growth via new customer acquisition, expanded geographic presence, or new channels

questions.prompt: After seeing Exhibit 1, what is the implied revenue target to quadruple profits?
questions.guidance: Current net income is $1.37M. Quadrupling profits means reaching roughly $5.48M net income. However, the more relevant framing for a growth case is operating income or a broader profit metric. A strong candidate notes that with operating income at $11.40M, quadrupling implies ~$45.6M operating income, requiring revenue of approximately $800M (given current ~5% operating margin), which represents roughly 3.5x current revenue. The candidate should conclude that cost reduction alone cannot achieve this — top-line growth is essential.

math.setup: Current net income = $1.37M; target = 4x = $5.48M. Alternatively using operating income: $11.40M x 4 = $45.60M. At current ~5% operating margin, required revenue = $45.60M / 0.05 = $912M. Rounded estimate often cited as ~$800M.
steps: Implied revenue at 5% margin: $45.60M / 0.05 = $912M (casebook approximates as ~$800M)
Current revenue is $229.24M, so required growth is roughly 3.5x to 4x
math.answer: Need revenue of approximately $800M–$912M, roughly 3.5–4x current revenue; cost-cutting alone is insufficient

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibits 2 and 3, what insights do you draw about the client's current revenue model?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 2 shows regional breakdown — South US sales are significantly lower than other regions, indicating an underpenetrated geography. Exhibit 3 shows product mix — the client is heavily weighted toward Disposable and Traditional lenses. A strong candidate asks: is there growth opportunity in Regular lenses (answer: market is saturated) or Cosmetic lenses (answer: not estimated to grow much), and flags South US as a potential geographic expansion opportunity.

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibits 4–8, which customer segments represent the greatest growth opportunity?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 4 covers total users (new adopters + existing users) — the candidate should recognize this is less useful for targeting since existing users rarely switch brands. Exhibits 5–8 focus on new adopters, which is where the client can actually gain share. Key insight: women below age 30 are the highest-growth new adopter demographic. Geographically, cities and suburbs in the South US are the fastest-growing and high-user areas. The candidate should explicitly set aside Exhibit 4 and build the argument from Exhibits 5–8.

questions.prompt: Given that optometrists drive brand choice for new adopters, what is the strategic implication?
questions.guidance: Since new adopters follow the optometrist's recommendation and existing users rarely switch, the client's growth lever is influencing optometrists at retail contact lens stores. A strong candidate frames this as a B2B2C strategy: target the optometrists (intermediaries) rather than end consumers directly. This should translate into a focused sales and marketing effort toward optometrists in high-growth areas.

questions.prompt: What is your assessment of international expansion as a near-term growth path?
questions.guidance: Western Europe and Japan are the only meaningful international markets, but competitors are deeply entrenched and the client has minimal presence. Building presence takes time. Given the 2-year horizon, international expansion is unlikely to deliver the required growth quickly. The client should monitor these markets for long-term strategy but focus near-term efforts on the US.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions should the client take to target the right optometrists and retail stores?

categories.name: Store location criteria
ideas: Stores located in cities and suburbs in Southern US
Stores in strip malls co-located with retailers popular among young women (e.g., major clothing chains)

categories.name: Customer demographic focus
ideas: Target stores whose significant customer base is young women (under 30)
Prioritize highest-growth geographic pockets within South US

categories.name: Optometrist engagement
ideas: Build direct relationships with optometrists at targeted retail stores
Create brand awareness programs and incentives for optometrists
Provide samples and clinical evidence to optometrists
Train sales reps to focus on optometrist-facing messaging

categories.name: Channel strategy
ideas: Strengthen retail presence in South US
Evaluate whether to grow online refill channel for acquired customers
Consider partnerships or co-marketing with retail eyewear chains

recommendation: To achieve rapid profit growth, the client should concentrate sales and marketing resources on targeting optometrists at contact lens retail stores, focusing on locations in cities and suburbs in Southern US where the client is underpenetrated and new adopter growth is highest
Priority stores should have young women as a significant portion of their customer base and be located in malls or strip malls adjacent to retailers popular with young women

This approach leverages the key insight that optometrists drive brand selection for new adopters — the segment where switching actually occurs — and that South US represents the largest untapped geographic opportunity
risks: Over-concentrating on the South may cause the client to under-invest in existing strongholds, risking share loss elsewhere
Competitors (Novartis, Bausch & Lomb) may already be entrenched in Southern US retail locations, requiring higher SG&A to displace them
Other competitors may simultaneously target the same high-growth South/young-women demographic, intensifying competition
International markets are deprioritized in the near term, deferring a potentially large long-term opportunity
next_steps: Map all contact lens retail stores in South US cities and suburbs; score by demographic profile and growth rate
Develop an optometrist outreach and relationship program for the top-tier stores
Establish KPIs for new-adopter acquisition by region to track 2-year profit trajectory
Conduct a competitive audit of competitor presence in targeted Southern US stores
Set a long-term roadmap for Western Europe and Japan entry once US growth is secured
